24岁，旧金山，一个中国工程师，被电视台堵在家里采访。他已经8个月没去过办公室了——所有会议、邮件、消息，全扔给了AI。

他原话是：“五个早会太要命了，让AI替我应付就行，我待在VR里。”

镜头在第25秒扫过他身后的架子：好几台笔记本叠在一起，每一台都对应一家公司的办公系统。AI在用他的语气和声音，替他在同事面前“演戏”。

五支团队对他的评价出奇统一：“这人反应快，回复也及时。”

而他本人呢？戴着VR头显，几乎8个月没动过手。五份工资，照常到账。

text:
I genuinely don't understand why everyone isn't using this yet

Andrej Karpathy, a co-founder of OpenAI, posted a simple idea that hit 16 million views: stop using AI to write code, use it to build a second brain.

You point Claude Code at a folder, drop in any source, an article, a transcript, a PDF, and Claude reads it, links it, and files it into a living wiki of everything you know. It compounds like interest, the more you feed it, the smarter it gets.

Here's the whole thing:

> Install Obsidian, create a vault, open it in Claude Code

> Paste Karpathy's wiki idea file and tell Claude to build it

> Claude makes three folders: raw for sources, wiki for its pages, a CLAUDE.md that runs it

> Drop any source into raw and say "ingest this"

> Ask questions across everything, forever

Five minutes to set up, and you never start from a blank chat again.

Full step-by-step guide with Claude and Obsidian, link below.

从《诗经》到近现代，三千年的中国文化被彻底结构化。 

每一首诗都有自己的空间坐标，李白是很亮的一颗星，但几十万个你从没听过名字的边缘诗人，也各自占着一个独立的坐标。

随手点开任意一颗星就能直接读诗，甚至还能看清整个历史文人圈子纵横交错的关系网络。

Codex 疯狂写磁盘的问题已经修复了 ✅

但 Codex App 暂时还没更新，需要手动更新 Codex CLI 到 0.142.0 才能解决问题。

两种更新方式：
方式一：在 Claude Code 里用 AI 帮你更新 直接输入提示词：
```search web & update codex cli```
让 AI 自动搜索并完成更新。

方式二：npm 手动更新
```npm install -g @openai/codex@latest```
更新完就不会再疯狂写磁盘了

text:
昨天在银行看见一位精神矍铄的老大爷来取钱。
他直奔窗口，气势十足。保安赶紧上前拦住，笑着说：“大爷，您先按号排队。”
大爷耳朵可能不太灵光，往前凑了凑：“啊？你说啥？”
保安提高音量，字正腔圆地重复：“按——号！”
大爷一听，眼睛顿时亮了，神秘兮兮地凑到保安耳边，压低声音回了句：
“天王盖地虎！”
保安愣了半秒，无奈地叹了口气，默默走到取号机前，帮大爷按出一张小票，塞到他手里。
大爷接过票，乐得合不拢嘴，得意地对周围人炫耀：
“不愧是大银行！取个钱还要对暗号，幸亏我反应快，蒙对了！”
说完还朝保安眨了眨眼，那表情仿佛刚完成了一场地下接头任务。
保安一脸生无可恋……

text:
英国脱口秀演员 Jimmy Carr 说了段大实话。

关于要不要孩子，他提到了一个特别扎实的人性机制。

他跟伴侣在一起很多年，一直没要孩子。
过去他总觉得，不生孩子简直就是人生这款游戏里的“终极外挂”。
超级简单，轻松愉快。

他以为自己活得很透彻，对这个世界也算得上“利益相关”。
直到后来，他有了孩子。
他才发现，自己以前全想错了。

他说：生孩子就像做了一场医学手术。
医生把你的心脏取出来，放到了你身体外面去生活。
从此，你的软肋、你的命门，就在外面跑了。

那一刻起，你才真正跟这个世界的未来锁死在一起。
你开始极度在意自己的寿命，开始害怕死亡。
以前，你觉得最惨的结果不过是自己死掉，没什么大不了。
现在，死变成了一件极其恐怖的事，因为你得跟孩子说再见。

Jimmy Carr 说：
“我以前以为自己是在用‘简单模式’打游戏，其实，我只是坐在一张筹码最低的赌桌上。”

“现在，我坐上了一张高筹码的牌桌。”
“虽然赌注巨大，但这也带来了真正的、无与伦比的快乐。”

这大概就是人生的某种隐秘机制。
人类设计出来，并不是为了追求绝对的“零风险”。
逃避筹码，确实能换来一时的轻松。
但只有当你把最珍贵的东西推上牌桌，真正跟未来产生连接时，那种极致的活着的感觉，才会真正降临。

text:
42岁的张师傅，今天工资到账8700元。
他先把银行房贷划走3600，又把逾期十多天的花呗还了2100，给妻子转了2000，给老母亲转了800，自己手机充了100元话费。
算完账，卡里还剩900块。他骑上那辆用了八年的电动车，决定犒劳自己一顿——去街口小饭馆，要了碗18块的宫保鸡丁盖饭，外赠一瓶冰可乐。
饭刚端上来，手机震动了一下。妻子发来语音，语气里满是兴奋：“老张！我给儿子报了个暑期兴趣班，编程+英语双科，一个月才3000！老师说这孩子有天赋，不能耽误！”
张师傅拿着筷子的手微微一抖，米饭差点洒出来。他盯着屏幕看了几秒，深吸一口气，把那口凉气慢慢压进胸腔，脸上重新浮起惯常的平静。
他把语音点成已读，回复了个“好的”，然后继续低头扒饭。
可乐的气泡在杯子里轻轻作响，像极了他此刻的心跳——表面平静，底下却翻涌不止。

text:
这速度真特么离谱啊！卧槽！

最新开源的Unlimited-OCR能一次性处理几百页文档，而且速度还很稳。

而这个模型来自百度刚刚在hugging face 发布，其核心创新是R-SWA（Reference Sliding Window Attention）。

它让模型在解码时KV Cache保持恒定，不会随着文档页数增加而爆炸式增长。

结果就是：一张图或者一本多页PDF，直接扔进去就能一次性解析完，速度和稳定性都比传统逐页处理的方式好很多。

在OmniDocBench上拿到了93分，比DeepSeek-OCR高出6个百分点。

这已经不是简单的准确率提升，而是把长文档OCR的工作流从“分块+外部调度器拼接”变成了真正的端到端一镜到底。

以前做多页文档最头疼的就是上下文断裂和格式不一致，现在模型能一次性看到整篇文档的结构、布局和逻辑关系，输出质量自然上了一个台阶。

这其实是把OCR从“认字工具”往“长文档理解引擎”又往前推了一大步。

技术路线很清晰，也很实用。
果然百度现在OCR独树一帜，遥遥领先了。

模型地址见评论区～ 👇

text:
“地址证明”是一个我至今无法理解的东西。住新加坡和香港的时候没少被它折腾

本质上来讲，它仅仅是一张印有我姓名和住址的纸。而由于银行登记的地址可以随便改，想改成什么都可以，从而它也不足以证明我“住在那里”

如果要用它证明我的实际居住地点，它的权威性远不如租房合同（但租房合同在绝大多数场景下又无法作为地址证明），而证明我逗留身份的合法性上又不如签证或身份证。从使用场合上来讲，仅仅是寄一些无关紧要的信件，通信的便利性和可靠性又远不如邮件/电话/短信

刚到新加坡时，由于之前错误多注册了一个 Shopee 账户，我想注销那个多余的账号，客服要我交地址证明。而因为刚到新加坡，银行账户还没开好，没有信用卡，电话卡月结单还没发出，水电单上是合租室友的名字，所以我提供不出任何能作为“地址证明”的文件。因此客服说无法注销。而无论是租房合同还是雇主开的地址担保信在 Shopee 客服那儿都无法作为地址证明。更讽刺的是，我当时的雇主就是 Shopee

后来在香港工作，申请安信和Mox 信用卡的时候，又因为提供的地址证明上的地址是酒店或者长租公寓而被告知不符合要求，我说这就是我在香港的长期唯一住所，有长租合同，印花税证明都有，客服告知总之就是不行，后来说填我朋友在香港的地址也可以... 好吧，也许要地址证明的机构也知道这个文件没有一丁点用处。真搞不懂为什么对这个文件的要求能长期存在😓

text:
通过 Vibe Coding 赚到了 10000 刀

https://t.co/SewSZ8KEkD 这款产品本身是我学习 Vibe 的过程里做出来的，现在差不多带来了一万刀以上的收益（当然营收都算公司的）。

谁说 Vibe 是写教程整玩具除了自己没用户呢？能做出有价值的内容，自然会有用户为此付费。

上线以来的开发节奏：

6/3–6/5 · 会员 Demo 视频 + 阅读列表同步连修，上线，修复各种小 bug。
6/8–6/11 · 用户态/认证健壮性
6/14–6/16 · 移动端响应式大改造 + 阅读器打磨

6/19 · 转发墨问功能上线 + 弹窗细节
一天 8 个 commit 把"转发到墨问"从无到有：新建 MowenShareDialog + mowenNote 构建/请求逻辑 + Reader/ReadingList  入口。上线后马上迭代细节——引语文案、去掉末尾明文网址、移动端去掉冗余「完成」按钮。垂直对齐来回改了好几版，中间还 revert 过一次，最后才定下来。

6/21–6/22 · 音频播放卡顿修复（三轮迭代）

未来还有系列迭代计划。其实主要是想清楚做什么东西，做起来是真的快，修 bug 反而慢一些 😂

text:
There’s a big misconception about how GLM 5.2 was trained. Yes, they distilled Claude and GPT 5.5 — but distillation is not how they matched Opus quality. Distillation only fixed the cold start problem in RL.

RLing an agentic coding model isn’t rocket science. In simplified terms:

1. RL needs trajectories — rollouts where the model actually completed a task in some env

2. No successful trajectory on a task = zero gradient = you can’t RL it. This is the cold start problem

3. Distillation solves it. You seed your model with knowledge from a smarter one (Claude, GPT) on tasks it can’t do yet

4. Now it produces positive trajectories on those tasks

5. RL on those trajectories and hill climb agentic coding

6. At that point you no longer need to distill and can solely hill climb RL to better models

This is an interesting curve. I’d argue it’s harder to get to Opus 4.8 from scratch than to go from Opus 4.8 → Fable/Mythos tier.

GLM 5.2 is already producing positive trajectories, so they have plenty to RL on — they’ll keep climbing to Mythos quality without distilling any further. They no longer need American models.

SAKANA FUGU ULTRA vs. CLAUDE OPUS 4.8 RESULTS

Prompt: "build a really high quality single html file crossy road game with three.js"

Sakana Fugu Ultra:
 - Tokens Used: ~89k ($7.32)
 - Time Elapsed: 22 minutes
 - Issues: inverted directional turn, wonky camera, no sfx, not identical to Crossy Road game

Claude Opus 4.8 Ultracode:
 - Tokens Used: ~940k (~$37.85)
 - Time elapsed: 79 minutes
 - Issues: got stuck twice in a retry loop (had to prompt to self-correct), wrong character position after restart, difficult from the start (whereas Fugu's version got significantly more difficult as you progress, which is the correct behaviour)

I think in terms of application functionality, quality, and design, Opus won. In terms of model speed and performance, Fugu on Opencode won. 

What are your thoughts? Comment down below who you think won! ⬇️

text:
一个工程师用 AI 把仓库路由子模块重写了一遍。代码更干净了，回归测试全绿，改动限制在子模块边界内。PR 发出去，被拒了。

拒他的人是在这套系统上工作了两年多的同事。理由很简单：你没和我对过设计，我看不懂新版本出了问题怎么排查。出了问题半夜被叫起来的人是我，不是你。

两个人都没错。一个看到旧代码是屎山，自己清理了一遍。一个看到自己负责的系统里多了一堆没参与讨论的陌生代码。

问题不在代码质量。问题在于：设计选择还没在团队里达成共识，就已经变成了几千行代码。

AI 把写代码变便宜了，但没有把设计取舍变便宜。过去写代码慢，慢这个缺点自带保护——它迫使团队在中间停下来讨论。现在你一天就能把一个设计假设变成几千行可运行的代码推上来让大家在 PR 里发现。

旧代码里那些看起来多余的分支，有一部分是技术债，也有一部分是事故记忆。AI 读到一个 if 语句，看不到语句背后那次全网雪崩的下午。重构时优化掉这些"冗余"逻辑，没有回归测试能抓到。测试验证你知道的事，验证不了你不知道的事。

解法不是去证明 AI 写的代码比人写的好。解法是把争论对象往上移一层：组织一次不看代码的设计评审。先回答这个系统为什么难、保什么、牺牲什么、出问题谁响应。把共识写成文档，再喂给 AI 按文档重写。

AI 写代码反正快，哪怕设计被推翻重做一版也没多少损失。你真正要珍惜的是团队共识，不是当前这版代码。

https://t.co/PUAcXjBNEC

text:
党哥这次真的退出推特了，退出之前宣布一个非常重要的事情。

高考结束这几天，如果你的孩子在A专业和B专业之间犹豫，比如电子、计算机、临床、电气等等之间犹豫，你需要做三件事：

1. 网上搜索清华或者北大对应的专业培养计划，比如电子、计算机、机械、电气等等，把大学四年的课程全部打印出来；

2. 打印到一张纸上以后，一门一门课问豆包、元宝、通义千问、deepseek、kimi、智谱（主打一个一碗水端平），一门一门课问，这门课的官方指定教材叫什么名字，把书名写在这张纸上面；

3. 带着这些课程培养计划和教材名字，带着孩子去你家周围最大的新华书店、图书馆、大型学术类书店、大学学校周边学术书店，带着孩子直接坐三天，一本本书翻出来看。

注意，不一定是清华大学那门课的出版社和作者，只要名字差不多就行，比如清华是张三的《数字电子技术》，你去书店里找James Bond的《数字电子技术》也完全没有问题。

比如孩子对电子感兴趣，6学分的《电路》，4学分的《数电》《模电》《嵌入式》《DSP》《CPU架构/微机原理》，帮孩子把教材找出来，让孩子翻看一遍，看看孩子感不感兴趣，

比如孩子对计算机感兴趣，找出来《算法和数据结构》、《操作系统》、《编译器》、《数据库》的教材，让孩子翻看一个小时，看看孩子愿不愿意学这些知识，

比如孩子对临床感兴趣，把《生理学》《病理学》《内科学》《外科学》这些书找到，让孩子坐在书店里翻一翻，看看孩子感不感兴趣，

比如孩子对电气感兴趣，除了数电模电以外，再把《电机和电力拖动》《交流调速》《电力电子技术》《工程电磁场》这些专业书翻出来，让孩子迅速翻一遍。

等孩子对基础专业课有个模糊的认知，再来决定选不选这个专业，

如果孩子一看模电就头疼，死活不愿意算与非门电路，那就趁早让孩子别学集成电路，老老实实学计算机，

如果孩子一看任何代码就难受，但是非常愿意看《内科学》《外科学》这几本书，那就踏踏实实让孩子学临床医学。

一定要把三四个孩子能接受专业的清华大学培养计划打印出来，找到教材，让孩子提前适应，提前有个了解，了解后再做出大学专业的选择。

切记，切记，切记。

比如孩子对电子感兴趣，6学分的《电路》，4学分的《数电》《模电》《嵌入式》《DSP》《CPU架构/微机原理》，帮孩子把教材找出来，让孩子翻看一遍，看看孩子感不感兴趣，

比如孩子对计算机感兴趣，找出来《算法和数据结构》、《操作系统》、《编译器》、《数据库》的教材，让孩子翻看一个小时，看看孩子愿不愿意学这些知识，

比如孩子对临床感兴趣，把《生理学》《病理学》《内科学》《外科学》这些书找到，让孩子坐在书店里翻一翻，看看孩子感不感兴趣，

比如孩子对电气感兴趣，除了数电模电以外，再把《电机和电力拖动》《交流调速》《电力电子技术》《工程电磁场》这些专业书翻出来，让孩子迅速翻一遍。

等孩子对基础专业课有个模糊的认知，再来决定选不选这个专业，

如果孩子一看模电就头疼，死活不愿意算与非门电路，那就趁早让孩子别学集成电路，老老实实学计算机，

如果孩子一看任何代码就难受，但是非常愿意看《内科学》《外科学》这几本书，那就踏踏实实让孩子学临床医学。

一定要把三四个孩子能接受专业的清华大学培养计划打印出来，找到教材，让孩子提前适应，提前有个了解，了解后再做出大学专业的选择。

切记，切记，切记。

text:
America’s standard of living has been in decline for decades.

There is a group of respected intellectuals — Charles Murray, Nicholas Eberstadt, Robert Putnam, and to some degree J.D. Vance — who paint the story of America’s decline as a failure of culture. In these narratives, we are in trouble because we abandoned the habits of thrift, work, and family formation. As a consequence, America’s families and economic lives are falling apart. The failure is in the souls of Americans, and the remedy is a moral reconstruction.

I have enormous respect for these writers. I think they are describing, with real precision, the sociological texture of what has happened. But I know they have the causation backward.

In America’s ongoing decline, the social scientists are adept at measuring the obvious signs of distress: drug addiction, gambling, prostitution, suicide. But these problems did not destroy our culture. These problems are a result of what has been destroying our country. And that is hard for them to measure because they are not looking at the economics behind these changes.

A culture of thrift does not survive a monetary regime that punishes savers.
A culture of marriage does not survive an economy in which young men cannot afford to form households.
A culture of work does not survive a labor market in which working-class wages have tracked sideways for 50 years while asset prices have gone to the moon.

The cultural problems — the lack of thrift, the abandonment of marriage, and chronic underemployment — are rational responses to our current economic environment. When the economy ceases to reward traditional male roles, the culture adjusts. 

You can see this clearly if you look at the exceptions. 

In every demographic slice of America where the Cantillon transfer has been positive — where the households in question have been recipients of the new money, not victims of it — the old cultural patterns are completely intact.

Upper-middle-class professionals in Bethesda still marry at high rates. They still form stable families. They still raise their children with discipline, invest in their education, attend their kids’ sporting events, and stay married into their seventies.

They did not suffer a cultural collapse, because they did not suffer an economic collapse.

It is the people who did not receive the new money whose culture has come apart. And that is not a coincidence. That is the causation.

If you want to rebuild America’s culture, you have to first rebuild the currency.

text:
我就有点不理解
为什么我的舍友明明都是专业前几，天天校队集训，全国打比赛的。
但是平时的话，就只会用个豆包，还只用快速模式，连专业模式都不用。
消遣除了抖音就是游戏，手机刷、电脑刷、平板刷。
白天学 CS，晚上CS。平时还玩玩瓦罗兰特、三角洲。
我从未听他们谈及过 Code X 或者自媒体之类的话题，就没有什么新鲜的事物了，前瞻的视野。
他们给我一种感觉，他们打所谓的竞赛，挣一点点绩点，跟他们打游戏是一个性质的。
单纯为了积分，为了胜负欲，然后很风流的谈起哪个哪个高手，人上人的感觉
我没听过他们谈及任何有关理想、目标或者规划和品味的话题，上大学两年了，校门都没出过几次，除了寒暑假。
我感觉跟他们相处就是很乏味无趣。
每天最多的事就是互相嘲讽，那个还在学，这个还在卷
反正除了学校那点破事，就没别的事了。
我不懂，是我想的太过了，还是说这是一个普遍的缩影…

text:
Let's go! We're out of stealth with @TolmoHQ!

AI is completely redefining how software gets built. And how it's being attacked. Helping define what security means for this new world was impossible to resist. We had to go back!

We’re building the AI agent fleet to secure production environments. Our security agents continuously work on a live production knowledge graph that connects data from code, cloud services, containers, databases, and third-party providers. 

Imagine high fidelity pictures of what you’re building, with a tracked history of changes at scale! 

Our team spent years on the offensive side, breaking into cloud services, kernels, or cryptographic implementations, as well as building observability and security solutions for thousands of customers in production at Datadog.

Over the last few months, we’ve raised $22M, led by Accel and Y Combinator, assembled a stellar team in San Francisco and have been iterating with our first 45 design partners. It’s go time! 

Joining me today to announce Tolmo: my cofounders @JbAviat, @poledesfetes, and @arnaud_breton, alongside @msuiche and our early team @wbeuil, @jimmycaputo, @cryptonitemmk, @theraniarnia, and @TylerHaydenSF.

We're psyched to embark on this new journey together! 

We're building Tolmo in the open, and we're looking for feedback. Would love to hear your thoughts about what we're building!

https://t.co/1UbONYeIne

text:
我妈突然对我特别好，天天给我煲汤

她说以前对不住我。我说怎么了，她说她给我买了套房。

我懵了，我一个月挣八千，哪来的钱买房。

她说贷款了，用我的名字贷的，六十万。

我说妈，你买在哪？

她说老家县城，四十万全款，剩二十万装修。

我说你怎么贷下来的？

她说，用你的身份证和征信，你去年把身份证放我这一周我办的。

我坐在沙发上算账，房贷月供四千

我工资八千，一半没了。

我妈还笑，说没事妈帮你供。

我看着她，突然想起来她前年用我姐的名字

贷了五十万买了辆车，车她开着，贷款我姐还了两年了。

我跟我姐打电话说了，我姐说你也跑不掉。

我说怎么跑？她说，我跟妈说你工资高，我没钱。

我说你工资比我高。我姐说不，你高。

我说那怎么办？她说，妈的钱花完了

贷款是我们俩的，她跑不了我们也跑不了。

后来我妈又用我弟的名字贷了八十万，买了第三套房。

她每个月收租，三套房的租金刚好够还三个贷款

她自己一分不用出。

她打电话跟我说：“妈聪明吧，钱不用自己出

房子是你们的名字，以后都是你们的。”

我没说话，她挂电话之前说了一句：

“你弟那套，等他结婚你们别争。”

text:
The Mechanism Is Worth Billions. The Delivery Model Is Still Broken.

For most of a decade, the case for serotonergic neuroplastogens lived in the conditional tense. On June 22, 2026, that changed. Definium Therapeutics reported a clean Phase 3 result in major depression. A single dose of its LSD formulation, DT120, produced an 8.1-point placebo-adjusted MADRS reduction at the primary endpoint, durable at twelve weeks, with no serious safety signal. The market re-rated the stock within hours. That the serotonergic system can drive rapid and lasting change in the brain is no longer a hypothesis. It is a Phase 3 fact, and capital is pricing it as one.

The same result that validated the mechanism exposed the model. Definium's drug is full lysergide, and the therapeutic effect arrives with the hallucinogenic experience. That has to be managed in a clinic, under supervision, for the better part of a day. Workable for a controlled trial. A structural ceiling for a commercial product. Every patient needs a supervised setting. Every dose consumes clinical capacity. Every payer confronts a cost of administration that has nothing to do with the molecule. This is the inherited constraint of the entire classic-psychedelic category, and the widest gap between what these drugs can do and how many people they will reach.

BETR-001 is designed to close that gap. It is a next-generation neuroplastogen engineered to retain the neuroplastic mechanism while removing the hallucinogenic experience that caps the market. That is the design intent, and what we aim to confirm in the clinic. If the profile holds, the result is a medicine taken at home. No supervised dosing. No clinic bottleneck. That is the line between a specialty therapy constrained by its own logistics and a franchise that can scale to the size of its disease.

@BetterLifeBio is advancing the molecule first in chronic cluster headache and chronic migraine, severe and under-served conditions with a defined regulatory path and long precedent for serotonergic ergolines, methysergide foremost. The psychiatric opportunity Definium just validated does not vanish. It sits in the pipeline as optionality, held behind a faster and less crowded lead.

The case follows from the asymmetry. Definium is the validated, de-risked, multi-billion-dollar expression of this thesis, near the finish line. BETR-001 is the differentiated expression of the same thesis at the starting line, carried at a fraction of the value, built to solve the one problem the leader has not. The mechanism question is settled. The open question is what a company engineered to fix the delivery model is worth as it converts that thesis into milestones of its own.

*BETR-001 is in preclinical development. Statements about its intended profile and potential advantages are forward-looking and subject to clinical, regulatory, and commercial risk. No assurance preclinical goals will be confirmed in human studies.*

text:
Can Tech Stocks Keep Outperforming?

Technology stocks have been outperforming for a long time. That’s how technology gets to be nearly 40% of the S&P 500 and the Russell 1000 and 60% of the NASDAQ 100. The concentration of the indexes in technology stocks is a function of how well they’ve performed and the performance has solid, fundamental roots. They continue to outperform this year, the AI boom the driving force now, but the outperformance of tech – and the underperformance of just about everything else – actually dates back to 2017. Ironically, while AI is driving today’s outperformance, it is also reversing the things that started the outperformance 10 years ago.

The period from 2017 to today has seen the technology sector outperform every other sector by a wide margin. In fact, tech is the only sector that has outperformed the S&P 500 over that time and the difference is kind of astounding. Technology stocks returned nearly 25% per year over that time while the index returned 14.7%. Seven of the eleven economic sectors generated single digit annual returns over that time while just three, other than tech, managed double digit returns: financials, industrials, and consumer discretionary. Most other times see roughly half the sectors beating the index and half underperforming.

What was the catalyst? There were actually two. The primary change was the maturity of the SaaS (software as a service) and cloud computing business models. Prior to this change, technology was a much more cyclical business. Companies went through capital intensive upgrade cycles in hardware and software. The shift to the cloud changed the industry from a cyclical, capital-intensive model to an asset light model that raised margins and reduced the need for capital. A secondary factor, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, allowed the tech companies to repatriate overseas cash and use it to buy back massive amounts of stock. Reducing the equity base raised all the returns on capital metrics and the stocks responded; higher return on equity indeed.

The problem investors face today is that the cloud computing companies are no longer asset light. Data centers are not just cloud computing on steroids and the necessary infrastructure investment is shifting the tech industry to an asset heavy, capital-intensive infrastructure model. The hyperscalers (Amazon, Microsoft, Google Cloud, Meta, Apple, Oracle, etc.) are engaged in a huge capital spending spree that is eating capital well beyond their available free cash flow. The most obvious example is Alphabet’s (Google) recent secondary offering of convertible preferred and straight equity of $85 billion. They aren’t the only ones changing direction; Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, Salesforce, Intel, Cisco, AMD, and Apple have all either stopped their stock buybacks or severely curtailed them. Meta is supposedly considering an equity offering of its own. And don’t forget the SpaceX IPO and the expected OpenAI and Anthropic offerings later this year. The age of shrinking equity is coming to an end.

Less noticed – at least by most equity investors – is the massive issuance of debt. The five major hyperscalers issued $120 billion in debt in 2025 and AI-related debt this year is expected to reach over $500 billion with almost $150 billion already announced by the big five. Return on equity is at an all-time high for the sector because of this new debt; the ROE/ROIC ratio sits over 6 for the sector. In addition, ROE has been goosed by all those stock buybacks shrinking the equity base since 2017. That is changing and will start to show up in a lower ROE over the next few years. With buybacks off the table – at least for now – the equity base will rise naturally due to employee equity/option grants. That will reduce ROE but ROIC will also compress due to increased debt. Furthermore, interest costs will reduce net income which will tend to reduce both ROE and ROIC. Tech stocks outperformed for ten years because of conditions that are now coming to an end.

Having said that, how tech stocks perform in the future still depends on whether they can produce an acceptable return on these investments. As you might have guessed, I have my doubts. These stocks today are priced as if the outcome is a foregone conclusion but there are a lot of ifs that can’t be answered right now:

Will the price of compute fall? If all the capacity on the drawing boards is actually built, I think the answer is obvious but will it be built? That’s a legitimate question as there are some powerful bottlenecks such as shortages of transformers, switchgear, cooling systems, battery backups, gas turbines, memory chips, and possibly the most critical, labor. Software engineers are figuring out how to achieve the same algorithmic results using vastly less compute. Through breakthroughs in model architecture, quantization, and small specialized language models, the amount of compute required to perform a task is dropping exponentially. If a task required 100 GPUs to process in 2024, but software optimization allows it to run on just 2 GPUs now, token prices may be irrelevant.

Will chips continue to advance at a rapid rate? If they do, will the hyperscalers be forced to continue their large investments? If chips are fully depreciated over 3 or 5 years, what’s the impact to reported earnings? Can Tech Stocks Keep Outperforming?

Technology stocks have been outperforming for a long time. That’s how technology gets to be nearly 40% of the S&P 500 and the Russell 1000 and 60% of the NASDAQ 100. The concentration of the indexes in technology stocks is a function of how well they’ve performed and the performance has solid, fundamental roots. They continue to outperform this year, the AI boom the driving force now, but the outperformance of tech – and the underperformance of just about everything else – actually dates back to 2017. Ironically, while AI is driving today’s outperformance, it is also reversing the things that started the outperformance 10 years ago.

The period from 2017 to today has seen the technology sector outperform every other sector by a wide margin. In fact, tech is the only sector that has outperformed the S&P 500 over that time and the difference is kind of astounding. Technology stocks returned nearly 25% per year over that time while the index returned 14.7%. Seven of the eleven economic sectors generated single digit annual returns over that time while just three, other than tech, managed double digit returns: financials, industrials, and consumer discretionary. Most other times see roughly half the sectors beating the index and half underperforming.

What was the catalyst? There were actually two. The primary change was the maturity of the SaaS (software as a service) and cloud computing business models. Prior to this change, technology was a much more cyclical business. Companies went through capital intensive upgrade cycles in hardware and software. The shift to the cloud changed the industry from a cyclical, capital-intensive model to an asset light model that raised margins and reduced the need for capital. A secondary factor, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, allowed the tech companies to repatriate overseas cash and use it to buy back massive amounts of stock. Reducing the equity base raised all the returns on capital metrics and the stocks responded; higher return on equity indeed.

The problem investors face today is that the cloud computing companies are no longer asset light. Data centers are not just cloud computing on steroids and the necessary infrastructure investment is shifting the tech industry to an asset heavy, capital-intensive infrastructure model. The hyperscalers (Amazon, Microsoft, Google Cloud, Meta, Apple, Oracle, etc.) are engaged in a huge capital spending spree that is eating capital well beyond their available free cash flow. The most obvious example is Alphabet’s (Google) recent secondary offering of convertible preferred and straight equity of $85 billion. They aren’t the only ones changing direction; Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, Salesforce, Intel, Cisco, AMD, and Apple have all either stopped their stock buybacks or severely curtailed them. Meta is supposedly considering an equity offering of its own. And don’t forget the SpaceX IPO and the expected OpenAI and Anthropic offerings later this year. The age of shrinking equity is coming to an end.

Less noticed – at least by most equity investors – is the massive issuance of debt. The five major hyperscalers issued $120 billion in debt in 2025 and AI-related debt this year is expected to reach over $500 billion with almost $150 billion already announced by the big five. Return on equity is at an all-time high for the sector because of this new debt; the ROE/ROIC ratio sits over 6 for the sector. In addition, ROE has been goosed by all those stock buybacks shrinking the equity base since 2017. That is changing and will start to show up in a lower ROE over the next few years. With buybacks off the table – at least for now – the equity base will rise naturally due to employee equity/option grants. That will reduce ROE but ROIC will also compress due to increased debt. Furthermore, interest costs will reduce net income which will tend to reduce both ROE and ROIC. Tech stocks outperformed for ten years because of conditions that are now coming to an end.

'The government had to step in and ban your product because it was too powerful.'

That's the best press release ever written. And the cheapest ad dollar ever spent. 

Fable 5 and Mythos 5 went under US Commerce export controls on June 12. The ban is still up today. 10 days of the entire AI community unable to stop talking about the model they can't have. I think the people writing Dario Amodei's professional obituary are reading this story backwards.

So, here's my take. I know what a bad product launch looks like and I know what it looks like when a product becomes the thing everyone wants and can't get. 

The week of the ban, every benchmark conversation started with Fable 5. Everyone that had three days with it before the controls hit was posting about what it could do. The ones who missed it were asking everyone who didn't. The hype was and still is real.

Then Dario shows up at a G7 on June 17. Sits down with Trump. Trump tells Axios afterward he no longer sees Anthropic as a national security threat. Anthropic's director of international goes on record: "very confident that in the coming days, the models will become available again."

I don't see this as a man whose company is in freefall. What I see is a man who's been working the room.

When Fable 5 comes back, Anthropic's valuation goes up. That's a given. The people who jumped ship and switched tools come running back. Demand spikes. Prices go up, limits come down. Mark my words, this will all happen.

Also, be prepared to see the posts about how much of a genius Dario is. Those will be coming too.

Enheduanna: The First Voice

Before Homer. Before Moses. 

A woman wrote 42 hymns, mapped heaven to earth through 42 sacred temples, and signed her name to the cosmos.

Her name on clay reads En-hedu-ana. 
High priestess. Ornament of heaven.

She was exiled. 
She was silenced. 
She was forgotten for four thousand years.

When archaeologists uncovered her tablets in the ruins of Ur in 1969, her name was still there—pressed into clay by her own hand. 

Waiting.

The first signature in human history. 

Rediscovered in the same year humans first walked on the moon.

As above. So below.

She did not describe cosmic order. 
She composed it. 

42 acts of devotion, binding heaven to earth, restoring what had been fragmented, expanding consciousness to the stars before the word consciousness existed.

What does it mean that the number she chose keeps appearing?

24|42

The Bank Surveillance Secrecy Act: How America Lost Financial Privacy | Free The Money Ep. 31

As we approach the United States' 250th anniversary, it's worth asking whether we've stayed true to the principles the country was founded on.

In this episode of Free The Money, I sit down with @EconWithNick, Research Fellow at the @CatoInstitute and Fellow at the @HRF, to examine the Bank Secrecy Act and how it transformed banks into de facto law enforcement and has led to decades of expanded surveillance every American.

Our Founding Fathers saw how general warrants were used to ransack people's homes, searching for anything authorities could use against them. They recognized this as a fundamental threat to liberty, which is why the Fourth Amendment was created to protect Americans from unreasonable searches and government overreach. Yet today, because of the Bank Secrecy Act, millions of financial records are collected yearly, monitored, and reported to the government without a warrant. What began as a tool to combat tax evasion has evolved into a vast financial surveillance system where banks have effectively become an extension of law enforcement.

Nick reported that in a single year, U.S. financial institutions spent an estimated $59 billion complying with the Bank Secrecy Act. During that same period, they filed roughly 28 million reports on their customers, yet those reports generated just 275 investigative leads for the IRS. Of those 275 leads, we don't know how many resulted in arrests or convictions. Nick argues these numbers are evidence of a broken system that subjects millions of law-abiding Americans to financial surveillance with very very little to show for it.

Building on that, we also discuss the Third-Party Doctrine, the legal theory that allows the government to obtain information shared with banks and other intermediaries without a warrant. What began as financial surveillance has expanded into something much broader. In an increasingly digital world, where nearly every transaction, communication, and interaction passes through a third party, this doctrine gives the government access to vast amounts of personal information that previous generations would have considered private. As Nick explains, the government is no longer ransacking physical homes, it is increasingly able to sift through our digital lives, collecting information that reveals who we are, where we go, who we associate with, and what we believe. The result is a level of surveillance that would have been unimaginable to the Founders, raising serious questions about privacy, government overreach, and the future of protections in the digital age.
